title: Event-Driven & Reactive Programming
summary: The paradigm where control flow is driven by events and streams rather than top-down execution — callbacks, observer/pub-sub, and reactive streams. The event loop's concurrency mechanics live in concurrency-models.

slides.markdown:
Every paradigm so far assumes your program controls when things happen — it runs top to bottom, or evaluates an expression, or answers a query, on its own schedule. **Event-driven programming** flips that: your code doesn't decide when to run, an external event does — a click, a message arriving, a sensor reading — and your code is just the reaction.

A button-click handler doesn't get called at a time your program chose; it gets called whenever the user clicks, in whatever order clicks happen to arrive. **Reactive programming** takes this further, treating a whole sequence of events — a stream — as a first-class value you can transform with `map`/`filter`/`debounce`, the way you'd transform a list.

This Topic covers the mental model — reacting to events/streams instead of running top-down. The event loop and async/await mechanics that actually *schedule* those reactions live in `concurrency-models`.

slides.sectionTitle: Reacting instead of running top to bottom
slides.markdown:
In every paradigm covered so far, your code's control flow is internally determined: an imperative program's next statement is the next line (or wherever a branch sends it); a functional program's evaluation order follows the expression tree. In both cases, *your code* decides what happens next.

Event-driven programming inverts this: you register a **handler** — a function to run when something happens — and then give up control. The runtime decides when (and whether, and how many times) to invoke it, based on events arriving from outside your program's control: a user action, a network response, a timer firing.

The mental shift this requires: you can no longer read a event-driven program top-to-bottom and know the execution order, because the order is determined by *when events happen in the real world*, not by the position of code on the page. Two handlers registered for different events can run in either order, or interleaved, depending purely on which event arrives first.

The simplest event-driven mechanism is the **callback**: a function passed as an argument, to be invoked later when the event happens. `button.onClick(handleClick)` registers `handleClick` to run on every click, with no explicit loop or polling anywhere in your code — the runtime's event system does the watching.

Callbacks compose badly once one asynchronous step needs to trigger another: `fetchUser(id, user => fetchOrders(user.id, orders => fetchInvoice(orders[0].id, invoice => { /* use invoice */ })))`. Each step nests one level deeper inside the previous callback, producing the infamous **"callback hell" / pyramid of doom** — deeply indented code where error handling has to be duplicated at every level, and the logical sequence of steps is obscured by the nesting structure rather than clarified by it.

This specific pain point is what later motivated promises and `async`/`await` (covered in `concurrency-models`) — they keep the event-driven *reaction* model but let the code read top-to-bottom again.

slides.sectionTitle: Event loop vs linear call stack
slides.markdown:
A traditional imperative call stack is a single line: `main()` calls `f()` calls `g()`, and each returns to exactly where it was called from, in a strict nested order — there's one active execution path at any moment.

An **event loop** looks different: a queue of pending events sits alongside the stack, and the runtime's main job is "take the next event off the queue, run its handler to completion, then check the queue again." Handlers run one at a time (in a single-threaded event loop like JavaScript's) but *which* handler runs next depends on which event arrived and got queued, not on any call relationship between them — `handleClick` and `handleTimerTick` have no caller/callee relationship, they're just two independent entries the loop happens to process in queue order.

This is why an event-driven program has no single "call stack you can read top to bottom" the way a linear imperative program does — the loop's dispatch order, driven by real-world event timing, replaces the program's own statement order.

slides.subTitle: The classic event-driven building block
slides.markdown:
Once you have events and handlers, you need a way for one piece of code (a **subject**, or **publisher**) to notify many independent listeners (**observers**, or **subscribers**) without knowing who they are in advance. That's the **observer pattern**: a subject keeps a list of registered observers and calls each one's handler whenever it changes or an event fires — `subject.subscribe(observer)`, then `subject.notify(event)` walks the list and invokes every observer's handler.

**Publish/subscribe (pub/sub)** generalizes this past a single object: publishers emit events to a named **topic** or **channel**, and any number of subscribers listening on that topic receive them, with the publisher never knowing who's subscribed or how many there are. A message broker (Kafka, Redis pub/sub) is pub/sub at system scale — one service publishes an `order.created` event, and any number of other services (billing, shipping, analytics) subscribe without the publisher coordinating with any of them directly.

Both patterns share the same payoff: the publisher/subject is decoupled from the number and identity of things reacting to it, which is what makes event-driven systems extensible without editing the source of the event.

slides.subTitle: Data as a first-class stream
slides.markdown:
Reactive programming treats a *sequence of events over time* as one value you can transform, the way functional programming treats a list as one value. A stream of click events, a stream of stock price ticks, a stream of keystrokes — each is a first-class object you compose with operators, not a series of individual callback invocations you write by hand.

`clicks$.map(e => e.target.id).filter(id => id.startsWith('btn-')).debounce(300)` reads left to right as a pipeline: take the click stream, extract each event's target id, keep only button ids, and suppress rapid repeats within 300ms. Each operator returns a *new stream*, exactly the way `list.map(f).filter(g)` returns a new list — the composition style from functional programming, applied to something that arrives over time instead of all at once.

This is why reactive libraries (RxJS, Reactor, Combine) borrow map/filter/reduce vocabulary directly from functional programming — a stream operator pipeline and a list transformation pipeline are the same idea, just applied to values that arrive continuously rather than values that already exist in memory.

Pitfall: losing the linear mental model
slides.subTitle: Callback spaghetti
slides.markdown:
The cost of event-driven code is exactly its benefit turned inside out: because execution order is driven by real-world timing instead of source-code position, **you can't debug it by reading top to bottom**. A bug that only appears when event A happens to fire before event B — but not the reverse — won't show up by re-reading either handler in isolation; you have to reconstruct the timing relationship between them, which the source code doesn't state anywhere.

This gets materially worse with nested callbacks: a bug three callbacks deep in a callback-hell chain means the relevant state is scattered across four different function scopes, each only reachable by mentally following the nesting, and an error thrown in an inner callback often needs its own explicit propagation path back to the top, because a normal `try/catch` around the outer call won't catch an error thrown asynchronously inside an inner one.

The practical mitigation most codebases converge on: flatten the nesting with promises/`async-await` (covered in `concurrency-models`) so the code *reads* linearly again even though it still *executes* in an event-driven way underneath — the mental model gets easier without changing the actual scheduling.

slides.sectionTitle: DOM events vs reactive data pipelines
slides.markdown:
| | Event-driven UI (DOM events) | Reactive data pipelines (RxJS, Project Reactor) |
|---|---|---|
| **Unit of work** | One handler per event type, registered once | A composed pipeline of operators over a whole stream |
| **Composition** | Manual — nest calls, or hand-write coordinating state | Declarative — `.map().filter().debounce()` chained |
| **Cancellation / cleanup** | Manually remove listeners | Built-in subscription/unsubscribe lifecycle |
| **Typical scale** | A handful of UI events per component | Potentially high-throughput streams (sensor data, market ticks, backend event buses) |

Both are event-driven at the core — something reacts to something happening — but plain DOM event handling was designed for a small, fixed set of UI interactions, while reactive stream libraries were built to make composing, transforming, and managing the lifecycle of *many* concurrent streams tractable, which matters once you're combining multiple UI inputs, timers, and network responses into one coordinated result (autocomplete-as-you-type combining keystrokes with debounced network requests is the canonical example).

"How would you model a live price feed updating a UI" is a standard prompt for this Topic, and a strong answer names the event-driven pieces explicitly rather than describing a vague polling loop.

A good shape: the price source is a **stream** of `PriceUpdate` events (one per tick), not a variable you poll — polling wastes cycles checking for changes that haven't happened and adds latency up to your poll interval. The UI **subscribes** to that stream (observer/pub-sub) rather than the stream knowing about the UI directly, so multiple UI components (a ticker, a chart, an alert system) can all subscribe independently without the price source being aware of any of them. Between the raw stream and the UI, insert transformations that matter for UX: `debounce` or `sample` so a UI update doesn't fire on every single tick if ticks arrive faster than the screen can usefully redraw, and `distinctUntilChanged` so a repeated identical price doesn't trigger a redundant re-render.

Naming debounce/sample specifically signals you understand reactive operators aren't decoration — they solve the concrete "my UI is repainting 1000 times a second for no visual benefit" problem.
